content.title: The Changing Landscape of Energy Supply
content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations

content.text: Lesson 2 Overview

This lesson explores the rapidly evolving landscape of global energy supply, influenced by the rise of renewables, shifting roles of fossil fuels and nuclear power, and the emergence of new energy carriers like green hydrogen.

It explains how market trends, technological progress, and geopolitical dynamics are transforming where and how energy is sourced, produced, and delivered.

Learners will gain insight into the expanding role of solar and wind, the uneven evolution of fossil fuels, the changing role of nuclear, and the promise and pitfalls of hydrogen in developing economies.

The lesson also highlights critical supply-side challenges from grid integration and mineral dependency to energy security risks. This will provide a forward-looking perspective on how energy systems must adapt to meet global climate and development goals.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: A: Projected Expansion of Wind and Solar PV

content.text: Renewable energy is poised to be at the heart of the future global energy system, with all major international institutions noting a significant acceleration in its deployment over the next few decades. While the pace, scale, and drivers of this transformation vary across scenarios, it is clear that solar and wind will dominate the expansion.

According to the IPCC, renewable energy is central to mitigation pathways aligned with limiting global temperature increase to 1.5°C or 2°C. In these scenarios, electricity from renewables is projected to grow from 28% in 2020 to 70–85% by 2050, with total renewable primary energy use increasing 6 to 13 times, from 57 EJ in 2020 to between 350–780 EJ in 2050 (IPCC, 2022). Solar PV alone could provide 36–70% of global electricity, and wind 12–38%.

content.quote: Nearly 100% of new electricity capacity additions by 2050 are projected to come from renewables in the 1.5°C and 2°C mitigation pathways.

content.text: However, this transition requires massive investments and rapid deployment, alongside systemic upgrades to accommodate variable renewables and ensure flexibility, reliability, and sustainability.

The IEA provides a nearer-term perspective, projecting that renewable capacity will increase 2.7 times by 2030, reaching 9,760 GW, with solar PV and wind accounting for over 90% of additions (IEA, 2024).

Annual renewable installations are expected to reach 940 GW by 2030, 70% higher than 2023’s figures, but still coming short of the global goal to triple capacity by the end of the decade. By 2030, renewables are expected to provide 46% of global electricity, with solar and wind together contributing 30%. China alone is forecast to provide 60% of global additions, adding more than 3,200 GW, while India is expected to be the fastest-growing large market.

The IEA also highlights the critical need to address bottlenecks as1,650 GW of renewable projects are currently awaiting grid connection, which shows the importance of infrastructure investments, permitting reforms, and policy clarity.

From McKinsey’s perspective ( displayed in the previous chart), the future energy mix will be dominated by low-carbon sources providing 65–80% of global electricity by 2050, up from 32% today (McKinsey, 2024).


This growth is driven by rapidly falling costs of technologies like solar and wind, which are already cost-competitive in many regions. Solar, in particular, stands out for its scalability and declining levelized cost of energy. However, technologies such as hydrogen and CCUS lag behind due to higher costs and limited policy momentum.


McKinsey also notes the opportunity for emerging economies to build renewables-based systems from the ground up, bypassing legacy infrastructure. But doing so requires intentional planning, robust institutions, and targeted policy and investment frameworks.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: B: Fossil Fuel Market Evolution

content.text:
The future of fossil fuel supply is characterised by a complex and uneven trajectory.

Among different scenarios from various organizations, some institutions claim that global fossil fuel demand may peak around 2030. But they are still expected to remain part of the energy mix for decades to come. According to the IEA’s NZE scenario, coal, oil, and natural gas demand all decline sharply after their peak.This transformation would reduce the fossil fuel share in global energy supply to less than 20% by mid-century, down from over 80% today (IEA, 2024).

However, current government policies and investment plans are not aligned with this pathway. UNEP’s 2023 Production Gap Report indicated that governments collectively plan to produce 110% more fossil fuels by 2030 than what is compatible with a 1.5°C scenario (UNEP, 2023).


Coal production, for instance, is projected to be 460% above 1.5°C-consistent levels according to UNEP, while oil and gas are projected to be 29% and 82% above, respectively. This significant gap risks expanding over time, driven by new infrastructure development and ongoing subsidies.

While coal faces the steepest decline, requiring near-total phase-out by 2040, oil and gas are also set to fall by approximately 75% by 2050 under the 1.5°C trajectory.

Other analyses suggest that fossil fuel demand will eventually fall but will still meet between 40–60% of global energy demand by 2050, down from 78% in 2023 (Mckenzie, 2024). Under many scenarios, 2030 is not a sharp turning point but a plateau in demand for fossil fuel, influenced by constraints in renewable energy deployment and the slow maturity of transition levers like industrial electrification, green fuels, and storage.

Beyond climate consideration, the transition also needs to address equity elements, as many developing and emerging countries currently rely on coal to expand energy access and drive economic growth. About half of the world’s oil and gas comes from these countries, which are often economically reliant on volatile fossil fuel revenues. In countries like Nigeria, Angola, or Mexico, fossil fuel income supports energy access and government payrolls, with public sector wages making up 30–50% of government spending across many African nations (WRI, 2023).

`For developing countries that rely on fossil fuels, this means an urgent need to begin planning for a just transition that protects workers, communities, and local economies. Key policy strategies include creating alternative sources of employment, investing in clean energy industries, strengthening social safety nets, and leveraging international financing mechanisms like the just energy transition 💬️ Partnerships (JETPs).

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: C: The Evolving Role of Nuclear Power

content.text:
Nuclear energy stands as a reliable low-carbon source of energy that is well-suited to provide baseload to the grid, referring to the minimum level of electricity demand on an electrical grid required for consistent demand.

But its contribution to improving energy access in developing countries remains to be proven and significant challenges remain to expand its capacity. As of 2023, nuclear accounted for just only over 9% of global electricity generation, generating 20% more than wind and 70% more than solar PV (IEA, 2025).

However, despite a modest 2.2% growth in generation in 2023, nuclear's global share has been on a declining trend from a 1996 peak of 17.5%, and its contribution remains limited relative to the rapid growth of renewables.


Still, some momentum is building. A multi-country initiative intends to triple nuclear capacity by 2050 to meet climate and energy security goals.

Currently, 63 reactors are under construction worldwide, representing 71 GW of new capacity, three-quarters of which are in emerging markets and half in China (IEA, 2025). Investment in the sector is accelerating, reaching USD 65 billion in 2023, double the level of a decade ago—with both new builds and refurbishments driving this increase.

In developing countries, nuclear energy is expanding but faces challenges. In 2023, nuclear accounted for only 5% of electricity generation in emerging markets and developing economies.

Nations such as India, Türkiye, Egypt, Bangladesh, and Pakistan are actively constructing nuclear plants. However for most African countries, infrastructure constraints are significant: It is recommended that a nuclear plant not exceed 10% of national grid capacity, a criteria met by only four African nations (IAEA, 2024).

Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) could offer a pathway, promising lower cost risks and shorter construction timelines, but most projects are still in demonstration phases and face delays and cost overruns.


Beyond electricity, nuclear may play a role in co-generation, providing both power and heat. For instance, China’s Haiyang project will supply district heating to one million residents, while India operates the world’s largest nuclear desalination facility (IEA, 2025). . These multi-use applications may contribute to climate resilience and industrial productivity in EMDEs.

Financing remains challenging as nuclear projects are capital-intensive with long payback periods, making them risky investments especially for developing economies.

Ultimately, while nuclear may contribute to clean energy transitions in countries with adequate institutional capacity, financing, and grid size, its global relevance may be limited, especially compared to renewable. From 2013 to 2023, nuclear power added just 247 TWh to global generation, compared to 3,508 TWh from non-hydro renewables (WNISR, 2024). Outside China, the sector has seen a net decline of 51 reactors and 26.4 GW in capacity since 2004.

Nuclear’s future depends on whether emerging technologies like SMRs can overcome financial and technical challenges and if they can do so fast enough to matter.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: D: The Role of Hydrogen

content.text:
Hydrogen is an energy-rich element that can be used as fuel or feedstock in various sectors, producing only water vapor and heat when used, but its climate impact depends on how it is made. Green (or Clean) hydrogen refers to hydrogen produced with little or no greenhouse gas emissions, offering significant potential for decarbonization 💬️ especially in industries.

Hydrogen might play an increasingly important role in the global energy transition, especially for decarbonizing hard-to-electrify sectors like heavy industry, long-haul transport, and aviation. By 2050, global hydrogen demand is projected to rise from 97 Mt in 2023 to between 111 and 614 Mt/year, potentially supplying 2–10% of global final energy consumption (Terlouw et al., 2024). But when it comes to clean hydrogen, less than 1 Mt of low-emissions hydrogen was produced in 2023, although planned projects could scale this up to 49 Mt/year by 2030 (IEA, 2024).


As deployment continues, production costs are projected to reduce by 50% by 2030, reaching between $2 and $9/kg H₂, with the potential to compete with fossil-based hydrogen (IEA, 2024). For developing countries, hydrogen offers both opportunity and challenge. The projected global hydrogen trade could reach $280 billion by 2050, with over half of this activity occurring in developing regions (IRENA, 2023). Africa and Latin America have vast potential to become low-cost green hydrogen producers. Latin America for instance could generate 7 Mt/year by 2030 (IEA, 2024). Hydrogen production could help reduce fertilizer import dependence and support local industries like green steel. However, realizing this potential will require a 20% increase in electricity generation in Latin America and significant upgrades to infrastructure, especially transmission.

However, unless green hydrogen strategies are rooted in inclusive planning and local benefits, they may risk replicating extractive models of the fossil fuel industries. In Namibia, for example, large-scale hydrogen ambitions are being developed in a country where 44% of the population lacks electricity access (World Bank, 2023). Diverting renewable energy toward hydrogen exports rather than domestic electrification could exacerbate energy poverty rather than alleviate it.


Additionally, the expansion of green hydrogen projects in water-scarce regions, such as North Africa and parts of Latin America, raises serious concerns. electrolysis 💬️ requires nine liters of purified water for every kilogram of hydrogen produced, and more than 70% of planned electrolyzer projects globally are located in areas already experiencing water stress (Fairley et al. , 2023). Without environmental safeguards, green hydrogen investments may deepen local inequalities, threaten ecological integrity, and reproduce patterns of displacement and marginalization.


For developing countries to truly benefit, green hydrogen must be pursued as a development strategy that centers equity, sovereignty, and long-term resilience.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: Case Study: China
content.subtitle: Developing Green Hydrogen to decarbonize hard-to-abate industries in China

content.text: Context

Rugao, located in Jiangsu Province in eastern China, is a mid-sized industrial city with a strong tradition in manufacturing and a growing commitment to environmental sustainability. As part of China’s national ambition to peak carbon dioxide emissions before 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality 💬️ by 2060 (BBC, 2020), Rugao was selected as the site of an innovative energy transformation initiative—the Hydrogen Economy Pilot Project—supported by UNDP and local partners. The project aimed to demonstrate how hydrogen could become a central pillar of a low-carbon economy, positioning Rugao as China’s first ‘Hydrogen City.’

The project was designed in response to ambitious climate goals and persistent structural barriers in the energy system. While China has made significant investments in solar and wind energy, challenges persist in areas such as energy storage, clean transportation, decarbonizing hard-to-abate industry, and domestic heating. Hydrogen, as a flexible and clean energy carrier, presented a powerful opportunity—but the country faced limited infrastructure, high production costs, few safety standards, and low public awareness. Rugao’s pilot project sought to address these interconnected challenges through a multi-sectoral and locally driven approach.

The intervention focused on developing a model Hydrogen City with clean hydrogen production, refueling and storage infrastructure, and applications across transport and domestic sectors. The implementation approach included a combined strategy of technology demonstration, policy innovation, capacity building, and knowledge sharing, executed through two interconnected pillars:

The ‘Brain’ focused on research, knowledge generation, policy development, and public outreach.

The ‘Body’ centered on real-world demonstrations of hydrogen technologies and systems.

The process focused on testing hydrogen solutions while building the systems, standards, business models, and human capital necessary for long-term adoption and scale-up. The project’s strategy consists of the following key actions:

Developing a hydrogen economy development roadmap to guide phased deployment: A strategic roadmap was crafted to guide the step-by-step rollout of hydrogen technologies across Rugao. It outlined priority sectors, investment requirements, policy milestones, and technical benchmarks for building a local hydrogen economy. This roadmap served as the foundation for all subsequent actions.

Establishing infrastructure for hydrogen production, storage, and refueling across Rugao: Following the roadmap, the project supported the development of green hydrogen production facilities, storage systems, and strategically located refueling stations to meet both public transportation and future industrial demand.

As a result of this strategically coordinated initiative, Rugao is emerging as a national leader in hydrogen innovation and was positioned as China’s first hydrogen demonstration city.

The project generated significant momentum through strong public-private collaboration, targeted policy development, and the deployment of real-world technology.

For example,
The Government of China mobilized a total of USD 10 M million in funding through UNDP to support hydrogen energy innovation, infrastructure, and demonstration in Rugao. This enabled the city to develop a functioning hydrogen ecosystem—from production and storage to refueling and vehicle integration.

Rugao was formally designated a ‘Hydrogen Featured Town’ by Jiangsu Province and selected by UNDP as a ‘Hydrogen Pilot City’, recognizing its role in spearheading China’s transition to clean hydrogen technologies. It became the nucleus of a growing hydrogen industrial cluster in the Yangtze River Delta. (UNDP, 2025)

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: E: Grid Integration Challenges

content.text:
As the world accelerates toward a clean energy future, grid integration is emerging as one important challenges of the energy transition. While electrification is surging, the power grids at the core of this transformation will need to undergo significant improvements.

Grid infrastructure is still largely designed for centralized, fossil-fuel-based generation and lacks the physical capacity and digital readiness to accommodate distributed, intermittent renewable energy sources. As a result, renewable projects may face delays, curtailment, and underutilization in the future, which may slow global progress toward net-zero emissions.

The scale of the challenge is vast.

Global grid line lengths are projected to increase by 15% by 2030 under current policies, and by 20% under more ambitious pathways (IEA, 2024). But grid projects often take over a decade to complete, far longer than the typical timeline for building solar or wind installations. Without corrective action, this disconnect may create structural challenges.

By 2030, investment in transmission and distribution infrastructure will need to rise to €550–750 billion annually, more than double today’s levels (IEA, 2023). From 2023 to 2030 alone, grid expansion rates must increase by 70% in the STEPS scenario, 90% in the APS, and 110% in the NZE pathway (IEA, 2024).

Even where physical infrastructure exists, power systems are being tested by growing demands for flexibility. Seasonal flexibility needs are rising 50% faster than electricity demand in Europe, 40% faster in China, and 30% faster in India (IEA, 2024).Climate change exacerbates these risks: in the Middle East, 90% of energy infrastructure will be exposed to over 20 additional days of extreme heat annually by mid-century. At the same time, the capacity factor of hydropower has dropped from 44% in the 1990s to 41% in the 2020s—reducing output by 330 TWh per year, equal to all new solar PV added globally in 2023.

A forward-looking grid must be smarter, more flexible, and better coordinated. Solutions include integrated grid planning using AI-driven models to simulate demand, weather, and asset failures. Smart connections, such as conditional access during periods of congestion, combined with transparent hosting capacity maps and standardized permitting can speed integration. Advanced grid technologies like digital management software, DER integration tools, and energy storage 💬️ will be essential.

Enabling these solutions will also require strengthened collaboration across regulators, utilities, developers, and consumers. Investment must also adapt : While $1 is spent on renewable capacity today, only $0.60 goes to grids and storage (IEA, 2024). By the 2040s, this ratio must reach parity. Without this rebalancing, the energy transition risks being slowed down.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: F: Increased dependency on critical minerals for clean energy technology

content.text:
critical minerals 💬️ are crucial for clean energy supply chains.

Demand for minerals like lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite, and rare earth elements is expected to surge. In 2024 alone, lithium demand increased by nearly 30%, while other battery metals grew by 6–8%, driven largely by the rapid deployment of electric vehicles, battery storage systems, and renewables (IEA, 2025). Under the IEA NZE Scenario, demand for critical minerals is expected to nearly triple by 2030 and grow to over 3.5 times the current levels by 2050, reaching nearly 40 million tonnes.

However, this rapid shift is exposing new energy security risks. Supply chains for clean energy technologies are heavily concentrated, with China accounting for more than 95% of refined graphite and rare earth elements, 70% of lithium chemicals, and over 80% of global solar PV manufacturing capacity (IEA, 2025). Globally, just three countries control 77% of mining and 86% of refining capacity for key minerals.

content.quote: If countries fully implement the national energy and climate pledges they have announced, mineral demand for clean energy technologies would more than double by 2030 and triple by 2040.
content.author: IEA, 2024

content.text:
Additionally, at the current pace of production, future supply may not meet growing demand for all critical minerals. For nickel, cobalt, graphite, and rare earths, planned projects could align supply with demand under current policies, if delivered on time.

However, copper and lithium stand out: copper may face a 30% supply shortfall by 2035 due to declining ore grades, rising costs, and long lead times. Lithium is well-supplied in the near term, but demand is expected to outpace supply by the 2030s.

For developing countries, this presents both opportunities and challenges. Nations like Argentina and Zimbabwe are emerging as new lithium suppliers, and Africa holds 25% of global graphite resources. Countries such as Indonesia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo are seeking to increase domestic value by implementing export bans on raw ores and investing in local processing industries. However, challenges remain: capital costs in emerging markets are around 50% higher than in incumbent regions.

Many critical minerals are also highly price-volatile and often produced as by-products, making them less responsive to market signals.
Addressing these risks will require proactive, policy-driven approaches. Governments are turning to tools such as price stabilization schemes, volume guarantees, and sustainability-linked market access standards. Technological innovation, including AI-enabled mineral exploration, could reduce drilling costs by 60% and improve discovery success rates (IEA, 2025).

Critical minerals will be crucial for tomorrow’s energy systems, but it is essential that their supply chains are secure, diversified, and equitably structured to support inclusive development.

To complement new supply and reduce pressure on mining, scaling up recycling of critical minerals will be essential to securing the future of energy systems. Unlike fossil fuels, critical minerals are not consumed but can be reused, offering a strategic advantage: a circular model of supply.

Today, recycled materials still make up a relatively small share of the market. For instance, the share of recycled copper in total supply has declined from 37% in 2015 to 33% in 2023, and for nickel, it fell from 33% to 26% (IEA, 2024).

By contrast, recycled battery metals, especially nickel, cobalt, and lithium, have seen rapid growth, with recovery rates reaching over 40% for nickel and cobalt and 20% for lithium in 2023.

content.quote: A successful scale-up of recycling can lower the need for new mining activity by 25-40% by 2050 in a scenario that meets national climate pledges. (IEA, 2024)

content.text:
Critical mineral recycling presents a major opportunity for a just energy transition.

Recycling not only reduces exposure to volatile global markets and import dependency, it also generates jobs, fosters local industry, and lowers environmental harm. In a scenario aligned with national climate pledges, recycling could reduce the need for new mining of copper and cobalt by 40% and of lithium and nickel by nearly 25% by 2050.

This would also avoid 30% in mining-related investment costs, an estimated USD 240 billion globally. For countries with limited reserves but growing energy demand, building recycling infrastructure offers a pathway to participate in mineral value chains without the high capital barriers of new extraction.


But today, the gap remains wide between regions: in Africa, formal e-waste collection rates remain around 1%, compared to 40–50% in Europe and North America. Unlocking this potential will require investments in collection systems, technology transfer 💬️, and supportive policies, such as extended producer responsibility and standards for recycled content. If well supported, urban mining and circularity could become powerful tools for resilience and equity in the energy transition.


Notably, they could help developing countries secure cleaner, more sustainable energy futures on their own terms.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: G: Geopolitical shifts

content.text:
Geopolitical shifts are increasingly shaping the future of global energy demand and supply.

One key example is the initial price shocks triggered by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, an event that continues to highlight vulnerabilities in the global energy system. Another example can be traced to the Middle East where global marine fuel sales increased in 2024 after disruptions to shipping in the Red Sea.

These examples also show how energy dependencies can become strategic vulnerabilities, and how political decisions and conflict can have ripple effects on energy worldwide. Since 2020, more than 200 trade measures affecting clean energy technologies have been introduced globally, which is five times more than the preceding 5 years, including new tariffs by the United States targeting segments of clean energy supply chains.

Today, most of the planned growth in clean energy manufacturing and processing is still concentrated in a few countries.

For instance, between 2023 and 2035, 50–95% of supply growth for refined copper, lithium, nickel, and cobalt is projected to occur in a few nations like China and Indonesia (IEA, 2024). China alone accounts for 85–95% of battery material manufacturing, over 80% of solar PV capacity, and 75–90% of the world’s processing capacity for minerals like cobalt, graphite, and rare earth elements. This concentration increases global energy security risks by making clean energy supply chains vulnerable to trade restrictions, geopolitical tensions, or localized disruptions in just a few countries.

Beyond clean energy, fossil fuel markets are also vulnerable to geopolitical disruption. Important maritime routes like the Strait of Hormuz and Strait of Malacca are crucial for global oil and gas flows, with the Strait of Hormuz handling 20% of global oil and LNG supplies.

As the global energy system becomes more electrified and renewable-rich, new forms of energy security risks are emerging. Unlike fossil fuels, where supply shocks hit consumers directly through higher operational costs, clean energy risks tend to raise the cost of deploying new infrastructure—like EVs or solar panels—rather than using existing ones. This distinction matters for policy responses and for how countries plan resilient energy transitions.


To manage these challenges, policymakers must recalibrate their understanding of energy security. This includes not only buffering fossil fuel supply but also securing critical minerals, diversifying clean technology supply chains, and anticipating bottlenecks in both traditional and emerging energy sectors. In an increasingly fragmented and unpredictable world, resilience and flexibility in energy planning will be just as crucial as supply itself.

takeaways.title: Fossil fuels remain deeply embedded in global energy supply, especially in developing countries where they support energy access and economies. This highlights the urgent need for a just, inclusive transition that protects livelihoods while phasing out carbon-intensive energy.

Renewables are transforming the global energy system, with solar and wind expected to dominate future electricity generation, but scaling this transformation requires massive infrastructure upgrades, policy reform, and investment.

New energy systems bring new vulnerabilities, from critical mineral dependencies to geopolitical risks and grid limitations, requiring smarter, more resilient supply strategies that are diverse, equitable, and aligned with climate and development goals..
